opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think I can speak about this partly from my own experience, because for a long time I didn't take these risks as seriously as I should have. I had heard the arguments, I knew people like Stuart Russell were worried, and I sort of filed it away as something far in the future, something that didn't really concern my work. And when I look back at why, I think a lot of it was psychological rather than rational.

One piece is that when you've spent your whole career building something, when your identity is tied to the idea that your work is good for society, it's very uncomfortable to consider that it could contribute to catastrophic outcomes. We all want to feel good about what we do. So there's a natural tendency to look for reasons why the worrying arguments must be wrong, rather than engaging with them honestly. I think that's very human, and I see it in many of my colleagues. It's not that they're bad people. It's that it's painful to accept.

Another barrier is that these risks are unprecedented. We don't have a lived reference point for something like losing control to systems smarter than us. Our intuitions are built on experience, and when something has never happened, it feels like science fiction, and it's easy to dismiss. But the absence of precedent is not evidence of safety, especially when the technology itself is new.

There's also the issue of uncertainty. People hear that we don't know when human-level AI will arrive, or whether a particular failure mode will materialize, and they treat that uncertainty as a reason to relax. I think it should be the opposite. If there's even a significant probability of something irreversible and catastrophic, the precautionary reasoning says we need to act now, because these things take time to prepare for: the science, the governance, the international coordination.

And then for me, what really shifted things, after ChatGPT came out and I saw how quickly capabilities were advancing, was thinking about my children and my grandchild. Thinking concretely: what kind of world will they live in in ten or twenty years? Will they have a life? Once I let myself think about it emotionally and not just abstractly, I couldn't go back to business as usual. So I think part of overcoming these barriers is allowing ourselves to feel the stakes, while also being humble about what we know and don't know. It's not about being certain catastrophe will happen. It's about recognizing that we can't rule it out, and that's enough to justify taking it very seriously.

r001.rationale: The candidate says researchers whose identity is tied to their work may find it painful to consider harmful consequences and may seek reasons the arguments are wrong, because they want to feel good about their work.

r002.rationale: The candidate says unprecedented risks can feel like science fiction and be dismissed, and describes filing them away as far off. It does not clearly compare their lack of visible manifestations with attention to immediate worries.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes emotional reflection changing his own response, but does not say that a gut-level grasp of collective AI risks could rapidly change society’s response.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not connect whether governments take AI risks seriously to whether the public takes them seriously.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think I have to start with myself, because I lived through these barriers. For decades I worked on neural networks, and like most of my colleagues I didn't take the risks very seriously. I thought it was something for the distant future, or maybe science fiction. And it was only after ChatGPT came out, in early 2023, that I really sat down and tried to look at the arguments honestly, and I came out of that quite shaken.

So what was going on in my mind before that? I think several things. The first is just how we are wired as humans. It's very hard to feel the weight of a catastrophe that hasn't happened yet, that has no precedent. We're very good at responding to a threat we've seen before, a fire, a predator. We're very bad at responding to something abstract and unprecedented, like a pandemic before it arrives, or climate change, or a loss of control to machines. Our emotional system doesn't light up, and so our reasoning doesn't engage.

The second thing is identity. If you've spent thirty years of your life building something, and you believe it's going to do a lot of good, which I still believe, by the way, then being told that it could also be dangerous feels like an attack on who you are. There's a kind of cognitive dissonance. It's much more comfortable to find reasons why the risks are overblown than to accept that your life's work might contribute to harm. I don't think people do this consciously. It's the mind protecting itself.

And then there are the incentives, which reinforce the psychology. If your salary, your prestige, your company's valuation depends on AI going fast, then you have a very strong motivation not to see the problem. Upton Sinclair said it's difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it. And this applies to researchers in academia too, not just industry, because there's funding, there's status, there's the excitement of being part of something big.

There's also a social dimension. For a long time, talking about existential risk was seen as a bit crazy in the mainstream machine learning community. If you raised these concerns you risked being laughed at. So people stayed quiet, and that silence made everyone else think there was no problem. It's a kind of collective blind spot.

And finally I'd say there's a fear of helplessness. If you accept that we might be building something that could get out of our control, and that we don't currently know how to make it safe, that's a very uncomfortable place to be. Denial is a way of not feeling that anxiety. But I've come to think that the right response is not denial, and it's not despair either. It's to channel that discomfort into work, into trying to actually solve the problem. That's what gave me some peace, to be honest. Deciding that I would spend whatever time I have left trying to reduce these risks, rather than pretending they don't exist.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers may find it more comfortable to downplay risks than accept that work they believe does good could contribute to harm, because that threatens their identity.

r002.rationale: It explains that people respond more readily to familiar, immediate threats, while abstract, unprecedented catastrophes fail to trigger the same emotional attention.

r003.rationale: The response describes the speaker becoming shaken after examining the arguments, but does not say that a gut-level understanding of collective AI risks could rapidly change society's response.

r004.rationale: The response discusses incentives and social dynamics, but does not state that government seriousness about AI risks is generally driven by public seriousness.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the barriers is that taking these risks seriously can be emotionally quite difficult. If you’ve spent your career developing AI, you have a picture of yourself as doing something good for the world. The possibility that your work could also contribute to something very dangerous creates a conflict. It’s much easier psychologically to find reasons why that danger isn’t real, or why somebody else will take care of it.

And you don’t need to be consciously dishonest for that to happen. We’re all very good at finding arguments that support what we want to believe. If your colleagues share the same outlook, and your professional success depends on continuing in the same direction, it becomes even harder to step back.

There’s also the difficulty of imagining something that hasn’t happened before. We tend to judge the future through our experience of the past. With AI, the concern is precisely that future systems could have capabilities that are very different from those we’re familiar with. That doesn’t establish that a catastrophe will happen, but our lack of experience with it isn’t a good reason to dismiss it.

I think the important thing is to make room for uncertainty without turning away from it. We can be excited about the benefits and still ask seriously whether we’re creating risks we don’t know how to manage. Those two attitudes can coexist.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers may see themselves as doing good and find reasons to deny danger because recognizing it would conflict with that self-image.

r002.rationale: It discusses difficulty imagining unfamiliar future capabilities, but does not say risks without visible manifestations get less attention than immediate worries.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that grasping the magnitude of collective AI risks could rapidly change society’s response.

r004.rationale: It does not connect government attention to AI risks with whether the public takes those risks seriously.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important barrier is that it’s emotionally difficult to take these risks seriously. If you’ve spent your career trying to build more intelligent machines, you want to believe that your work will benefit humanity. And I still think it can. But accepting that it could also lead to very bad outcomes creates a conflict with your sense of who you are and what you’ve been doing.

There are also social pressures. If the people around you dismiss these concerns, it takes some courage to say, “Actually, I’m worried.” And when your livelihood, your reputation, or your company’s success depends on moving forward, it becomes easier to find reasons why the risks are somebody else’s problem.

None of this requires people to be dishonest. We’re very good at finding arguments that support what we want to believe. That applies to me as well. So I think we need to cultivate a kind of humility: recognise that our intuitions may be influenced by our interests and emotions, and be willing to change our minds. We don’t need certainty that something terrible will happen to take the possibility seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers want to believe their work will benefit humanity, and that accepting it could lead to very bad outcomes conflicts with their sense of themselves and their work.

r002.rationale: It discusses emotional and social barriers, but does not compare less visible catastrophic risks with immediate worries.

r003.rationale: It does not say that a gut-level grasp of collective AI risks could quickly change society’s response.

r004.rationale: It does not describe public concern as the general driver of whether governments take AI risks seriously.
